In this work, we investigate probability calibration and uncertainty-aware selective prediction for emotion classification using a Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT)-based model. Experiments are conducted on the Emotions dataset, which exhibits natural class imbalance across six emotion categories. We adopt a multi-stage pipeline comprising dataset preparation, baseline fine-tuning, post-hoc probability calibration via temperature scaling, uncertainty estimation using probability-based metrics, and selective prediction based on uncertainty thresholds. Results show that temperature scaling further improves probability calibration, reducing expected calibration error from 0.0051 to 0.0035 (a relative reduction of approximately 31%) and tightening reliability diagrams, without degrading classification accuracy. Uncertainty measures such as predictive entropy and probability margin effectively distinguish correct from incorrect predictions, with misclassified samples exhibiting higher uncertainty. Leveraging these uncertainty estimates, selective prediction achieves a favorable risk-coverage trade-off: predictive risk decreases while accuracy on the accepted subset increases as coverage is reduced. At an operating point of approximately 90% coverage, the model attains substantially improved reliability with minimal loss in coverage. These findings demonstrate that calibrated uncertainty estimates enable robust selective prediction and provide a principled framework for deploying emotion classification systems in reliability-critical applications.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.2139\/ssrn.7225999","type":"posted-content","created":{"date-parts":[[2026,8,4]],"date-time":"2026-08-04T10:56:13Z","timestamp":1785840973000},"source":"Crossref","is-referenced-by-count":0,"title":["Reliability-aware BERT-based Emotion Classification via Probability Calibration and Selective Prediction"],"prefix":"10.2139","author":[{"ORCID":"https:\/\/orcid.org\/0009-0000-9317-340X","authenticated-orcid":true,"given":"Nisreen","family":"Albzour","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"member":"78","deposited":{"date-parts":[[2026,8,4]],"date-time":"2026-08-04T10:56:13Z","timestamp":1785840973000},"score":23.811443,"resource":{"primary":{"URL":"https:\/\/www.ssrn.com\/abstract=7225999"}},"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"references-count":0,"URL":"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.2139\/ssrn.7225999","published":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"subtype":"preprint"},{"indexed":{"date-parts":[[2026,8,24]],"date-time":"2026-08-24T19:27:53Z","timestamp":1787599673234,"version":"build-2736575974"},"posted":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"group-title":"SSRN","reference-count":0,"publisher":"Elsevier BV","license":[{"start":{"date-parts":[[2026,1,1]],"date-time":"2026-01-01T00:00:00Z","timestamp":1767225600000},"content-version":"unspecified","delay-in-days":0,"URL":"https:\/\/www.uspto.gov\/ip-policy\/copyright-policy\/copyright-basics"}],"content-domain":{"domain":[],"crossmark-restriction":false},"abstract":"<jats:p>Automated skin-lesion classifiers now approach ceiling performance on benchmark data, yet aggregate accuracy revealslittle about when an individual prediction can be trusted \u2014 the property that governs safe clinical use. We reframedermoscopic classification as a reliability-aware selective-prediction problem: rather than only maximizing accuracy,we ask when a model should commit to a prediction and when it should defer to a clinician. The proposed frameworkis evaluated on two publicly available dermoscopic datasets: HAM10000 and the Skin Cancer (ISIC 2018): Malignantvs. Benign dataset. On HAM10000, comprising 10,015 images, we train transparent tree-ensemble classifiers equippedwith a lightweight, retraining-free reliability layer combining maximum class confidence, predictive entropy, post-hoctemperature scaling, and confidence\/entropy-based accept\u2013defer rules. Although raw performance on HAM10000 is deliberatelymodest (accuracy 0.709; balanced accuracy 0.395 under severe class imbalance), the reliability layer is highlyinformative: maximum confidence detects incorrect predictions with AUROC 0.811, and temperature scaling reducesexpected calibration error from 0.120 to 0.028 (76.5% reduction). As a decision-support filter, accepting only the mostreliable half of cases raises accepted-case accuracy to 0.905 while routing 83.7% of all errors to expert review. Critically,global confidence deferral is majority-class driven and would still miss many melanomas, whereas a malignancy-awarereferral rule reduces the melanoma miss rate from 26.9% to 7.6% at matched coverage and below 1% at higher deferral.To assess generalizability, the same reliability framework is additionally evaluated on the Skin Cancer (ISIC 2018):Malignant vs. Benign dataset, which comprises 3,297 dermoscopic images, yielding a total of 13,312 images acrossboth cohorts. Reliability behavior remains consistent across datasets: temperature scaling reduces expected calibrationerror from 0.116 to 0.025 on ISIC 2018 (78.2% reduction), confidence-based error detection achieves AUROC 0.817,and selective prediction raises accepted-case accuracy to 0.967 at 50% coverage. These results show that reliabilityassessment, calibration correction, uncertainty-based error detection, and class-aware referral can transform probabilisticclassifiers into more trustworthy decision-support triage recognition in children\u2019s drawings is difficult because affect is carried by sparse strokes, symbolic objects, and overall composition rather than by the stable appearance statistics of photographs. Work in this area typically reports a single accuracy figure, which says little about which predictions can be trusted. We built a reproducible four-class benchmark (Angry, Fear, Happy, Sad) on an existing public corpus of 818 children\u2019s drawings and compared three transfer-learning regimes under identical stratified five-fold splits with nested model selection: ResNet-50, ViT-B\/16, and an end-to-end fine-tuned SigLIP image encoder (SigLIP-FT). Reliability was assessed using top-1\u2013top-2 probability margins, expected calibration error (ECE), and margin-based selective prediction. Five annotators independently labeled all images under a pre-specified analysis plan, providing a human reference point on the same items. SigLIP-FT reached the highest macro-F1 (0.773\u00b10.028) ahead of ViT-B\/16 (0.700\u00b10.040) and ResNet-50 (0.598\u00b10.038), and was the best calibrated (ECE 0.119). Margin-based abstention raised its macro-F1 to 0.818 at 73.0% coverage and 0.867 at 55.0%. Fear was also the least reliably judged category for annotators (Krippendorff\u2019s \u03b1=0.422), yet their majority vote recovered the corpus labels with macro-F1 0.960, well above the model. Coverage\u2013performance behavior, rather than a single full-coverage score, is therefore the appropriate reporting standard for ambiguous visual domains of this kind.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.20944\/preprints202607.2392.v1","type":"posted-content","created":{"date-parts":[[2026,8,6]],"date-time":"2026-08-06T01:32:22Z","timestamp":1785979942000},"source":"Crossref","is-referenced-by-count":0,"title":["How Reliable Is Automatic Emotion Classification in Children\u2019s Drawings?
